entry.title: Welcome to 3P: Physics, Psyche, and Python

link.title: Welcome to 3P: Physics, Psyche, and Python

entry.content:
Three letters. Three disciplines. One notebook.

This is the first post on what I’m calling 3P—an experiment in keeping my technical work, research reflections, and interdisciplinary curiosities in one place.

What 3P means

The name is deliberately compact because it captures the three directions I keep orbiting:

  • Physics: The patterns that govern systems, from particles to planets.
  • Psyche: The mind, cognition, behavior, and everything that makes humans complex.
  • Python: The language I use to turn ideas into code, analysis, and visual stories.

I don’t claim expertise in any of these domains. But I’m studying all of them—formally through my data science degree at NUST SEECS, and informally through the projects and questions that pull me off the beaten path.

Why I built this site

I wanted something that felt more like a personal publication than a static CV. A place where:

  • Project notes live next to technical write-ups
  • Code snippets sit alongside conceptual reflections
  • Learning logs show process, not just polished results

The portfolio pages you’ll find here (About, Projects, Contact) give the quick version of who I am. The blog is where I unpack the longer version—what I’m building, what I’m reading, what I’m trying to figure out.

What to expect going forward

I’m planning to post about:

  • My data science and machine learning projects (with code and commentary)
  • Notes on the research I’m exploring for my degree
  • Reflections on how psychology and physics intersect with data work
  • Occasional essays on philosophy, learning, and how I approach problems

Some posts will be technical. Some will be speculative. Some might just be me thinking out loud.

That’s intentional. A notebook shouldn’t be too tidy.

This isn’t an archive

I want this site to feel alive—more like a working journal than a museum of finished work. That means the structure might shift over time. The writing might get rough around the edges. The ideas might evolve mid-post.

And that’s fine. The point is to document, not to impress.

If that sounds useful to you, follow along. If you have thoughts, reach out. And if you’re just here for the code, I’ve got plenty of that too.

Let’s get started.

Next post: A proper deep-dive into the AirVision project I’ve been working on—how I built it, what I learned, and where it’s going next.

entry.title: AirVision 2026: Turning Satellite Data into a Cleaner Story

link.title: AirVision 2026: Turning Satellite Data into a Cleaner Story

entry.content:
AirVision started as a simple question: can satellite and reanalysis data make air quality easier to understand across multiple cities, instead of leaving it buried in raw tables and charts?

What I built

I built a Streamlit app that compares air-quality signals across 15 Pakistani cities and turns them into a visual study. The goal was not only to display data, but to make the differences easier to inspect and explain.

The project combines data collection, cleaning, feature engineering, and visualization. I used satellite and reanalysis sources such as Google Earth Engine, Sentinel-5P, ERA5, and CAMS, then organized the results into a small interface for exploration.

Why this project mattered

The main challenge in a project like this is that environmental data is rarely clean or immediately comparable. Different sources have different scales, sampling patterns, and noise characteristics. That means the real work is not just plotting, but deciding how to align the data so the comparison is meaningful.

That is the part I found most useful to work through. It forced me to think about data consistency, feature selection, and the difference between a dataset that exists and a dataset that is actually readable.

What I learned

  • Raw environmental data needs more interpretation than it first appears to need.
  • A good interface can make a technical project feel much more approachable.
  • The strongest part of a project is often the reasoning behind the pipeline, not just the final model or chart.

What I would improve next

If I extend the project, I would add clearer comparisons across time, stronger annotation of anomalies, and a short write-up explaining the assumptions behind each data source.

That would move the work even closer to a publication-style project rather than just a dashboard.
